Main concerns: token cost, fallback behavior on failures, streaming experience for editors, and security (data retention / KMS). AE Maya and SE Luis demo the Redwood Gen sandbox (hosted API + Console + Optimize) showing streaming chunks, parameter tuning, retry/fallback flows with shorter model, and a budget example for monthly token spend. Customer asks for pilot pricing and technical benchmarks.

- Parameters: max_tokens, top_p/temp, stop sequences, truncation, token budget heuristics
- Retries: idempotency keys, exponential backoff, fallback to smaller model on capacity errors
- Cost controls: Optimize suggestions, batching, KV caching (spoken as "KV cash" once), and token budgeting spreadsheet

Transcript body (timestamps are approximate; transcription imperfect):
[00:00] Maya (AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining. super quick intro, im Maya, im the AE on this account, with Luis who is our solutions engineer. how's everyone doing?
[00:09] Sarah (CTO): good, thanks. ran outta coffee but i'm here.
[00:12] Priya (Product): morning, thanks for scheduling. we're excited to see streaming and the cost examples.
[00:18] Maya: awesome. agenda — quick qual, then live demo of the hosted gen sandbox, parameter playbook, and failure/retry patterns. we'll leave time for q's.
[00:28] Rajiv (Lead ML Eng): quick qual first — we expect about 300 concurrent users at peak, but most requests are short single-turn messages, average 120 tokens out, maybe 60 tokens in. p99 latency target is 200-400 ms ideally.
[00:42] Luis (SE): cool, that's helpful. 300 concurrent with ~120 tokens output maps well to our hosted medium model families; we may suggest batching windows to improve cost. couple clarifying q's: are you ok with soft SLOs or is it strict SLA-backed?
[00:54] Sarah: initially soft, but we'll need predictable behavior for a pilot before committing to reserved. legal will ask about retention and KMS.
[00:59] Maya: noted. we'll follow up with SOC2 / KMS docs.
[01:05] Luis: ok jumping into the sandbox. sharing my screen — this is the Redwood Console, gen sandbox, you can see the model dropdown, streaming toggle, and params panel.
[01:20] [screen noise]
[01:23] Luis: i'll send a quick prompt: "Summarize this article for an editor in 3 bullets" — hitting run with streaming on. you'll see chunks arrive via SSE.
[01:34] Speaker 1 (auto): (inaudible)
[01:36] Luis: first chunk arrives ~80ms after request, then continuous chunks. you can see the stream chunks are partial and the client can render progressively. for editors this means they feel instant even if generation continues.
[01:48] Priya: is there a way to control chunk size or flush frequency?
[01:52] Luis: not directly a 'chunk size' knob; chunks are influenced by model tokenization and max_new_tokens plus our streaming framing. however you can tune max_tokens to encourage shorter outputs, or use stop sequences to force earlier flushes. also Optimize tab can suggest param combos for a given target latency.
[02:10] Rajiv: what's the worst-case? sometimes editors need the whole structured output, not partial. any guarantees?
[02:16] Luis: we don't promise chunk size deterministic, but we offer 'streaming=false' to wait for complete response. there's a tradeoff: blocking until full response raises tail latency. many teams use progressive render for UX.
[02:29] Sarah: mmh, ok. talk about retries — we often get transient 5xx from cloud endpoints. how do you recommend implementing client retries without duplicating work or overcharging?
[02:41] Maya: two parts — idempotency keys and safe retries. we recommend an idempotency header per user request to dedupe. for cost you can use our cost-estimate header and then do exponential backoff on 502/503, fallback to smaller model on capacity errors. Luis will show an example.
[02:58] Luis: demoing a simulated 503 and fallback. watch the sandbox: first request hits the main model, we simulate a capacity error, the client retries with the same idempotency key and sets model=babbage-quant (smaller). response comes back, no duplicate billing because the provider recognizes the idempotency token. note: some SDKs handle this for you.
[03:24] Priya: the 'idempotency header' — what format? UUID?
[03:27] Luis: yeah a UUID or hash of the request body is common. we call out X-Idempotency-Key in our client examples.
[03:32] Rajiv: you're referencing fallbacks to smaller models — how do we manage quality regressions? we'd rather degrade gracefully, not churn users.
[03:39] Luis: good point. our recommendation: maintain a model family map per route — primary high-quality model, fallback shorteners mapped. also implement response-level checks (e.g., if summary length < threshold or hallucination score high, then escalate or requeue). Redwood Optimize can run a quick A/B on small sample prompts to show quality delta.
[03:58] Sarah: is there tooling to detect 'meaningful' regressions? like content quality dropoff?
[04:02] Luis: Optimize has eval harness integration — you can attach prompt sets and expected assertions, and get regression alerts if fallback variance exceeds thresholds. it's not magical but helps catch systematic issues.
[04:15] [crosstalk]
[04:18] Unknown Speaker - finance: can you show token cost for a 1M monthly user base?
[04:22] Maya: sure, quick sketch. if you assume avg 180 tokens per session (in+out) and 2M sessions we can show a token-budget tab. Luis opens a sample spreadsheet in the console.
[04:38] Luis: here's a tokenizer view — shows tokens per request and estimated cost per model. you can toggle quantized vs full-precision pricing. one trick: use KV caching for repeated prefixes, e.g., system prompts, which cuts cost per token for longs. (said "KV cash" accidentally).
[04:58] Priya: can you remind us of caching limitations? we sometimes have dynamic user-specific context.
[05:02] Luis: KV cache works best for repeated system or rubric text. for user-specific context, you can cache partial completions or use a local embedding cache. batching also reduces per-token cost for many small requests.
[05:15] Rajiv: what about rate limits — if we burst we don't want throttling to break editors.
[05:20] Maya: hosted tiers have soft rate limits; dedicated/reserved capacity avoids throttles. for pilot, we can enable burst windows. also we recommend smart client-side backpressure and queuing.
[05:33] Sarah: let's talk security quickly. can you confirm data at rest encryption and KMS integration?
[05:38] Luis: yes — we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for private deployment and hosted with Bring-Your-KMS for enterprise. we also export audit logs and retention options. i'll drop the SOC2 and KMS whitepaper after this call.
[05:51] [00:05 silence, typing sounds]
[06:00] Luis: back to retries — demoing exponential backoff example in code. here's pseudocode: try request with idempotency key; on 502/503 retry with increasing delay; after N attempts fallback to smaller model. if still failing, queue request and surface to ops.
[06:18] Rajiv: if we queue for editors, we need a visible UX state; queueing for minutes is not acceptable.
[06:24] Priya: yes, editors need perceived instant. maybe degrade to cached summary or instruct user.
[06:29] Luis: exactly — graceful degradation strategies: 1) cached content, 2) summary from smaller model, 3) offline job with email when ready. important to define user expectation.
[06:42] Maya: quick nod to idempotency + billing: if you retry with same idempotency key and it eventually succeeds, Redwood's billing shows a single completed invocation. if multiple distinct requests are sent, billing will reflect that.
[06:56] Sarah: ok what about the SDK behavior for streaming and reconnects — if network blips, can the SDK reattach?
[07:03] Luis: our SDK supports resuming streams in some cases by replaying the last token index, but it's model-dependent. common pattern: client buffers last event id, if reconnects happen request with last_token_index and server can replay rest. not perfect for all models.
[07:22] Priya: sounds a bit fragile. any recommended patterns?
[07:25] Luis: best practice is to keep chunks idempotent and render progressively; on reconnect either request remaining tokens or fallback to full request. plus exponential backoff on reconnect attempts.
[07:38] Rajiv: what about concurrency limit per API key? we want to put a single key in the app; will that create hot spots?
[07:44] Maya: you can use route keys or split keys per shard; Redwood supports per-route routing and quotas, so you can distribute load across multiple API keys or route tokens.
[07:58] Rajiv: ok good.
[08:02] Luis: showing Optimize tab now — it suggests param sets when you enter target latency and cost. here's a sample: target 250ms p99, it suggests model X-2 quantized, max_tokens=120, top_p=.9, temperature=.2, and recommends prefix caching. you can export these suggestions to the console as a 'policy'.
[08:26] Priya: can Optimize create A/B rollouts?
[08:29] Luis: yes, it can push canary rollouts with traffic splits and automatic rollback on error or quality regressions. we demo a 10/90 canary and the rollback triggers on p95 latency spike.
[08:44] Sarah: ok back to cost: what's an expected monthly delta between hosted and dedicated?
[08:49] Maya: depends heavily on utilization. hosted per-token can be higher at low volume but easier to start; dedicated has lower unit costs but committed spend. we'll put numbers in the pricing doc.
[08:59] Unknown Speaker - finance: do you have discount brackets?
[09:01] Maya: yes, volume tiers and committed terms; we'll include sample scenarios in the follow-up.
[09:07] [silence]
[09:10] Rajiv: small deep-dive q — how do you measure 'hallucination score' you mentioned earlier?
[09:14] Luis: we compute heuristics: n-gram overlap vs knowledge sources, factuality checks via reranker, and custom assertion tests in Optimize. it's heuristic and must be tuned.
[09:25] Priya: any integration with our existing eval infra? we use an internal harness.
[09:29] Luis: yes you can upload your harness outputs or connect S3/GS buckets; Optimize will run jobs against the prompt set and push metrics back.
[09:38] Sarah: ok wrapping up — high-level recap?
[09:41] Maya: recap: Redwood hosted can meet your latency targets with param tuning and streaming; use idempotency keys for retries, fallback to smaller model for capacity failures, and use Optimize for param suggestions and regression monitoring. action items: we'll send pricing and docs, Luis will send bench scripts, customer will provide prompts.
[09:58] Rajiv: sounds good. question on timeline — pilot can start next week if we get the PoC scope and pricing.
[10:04] Maya: we'll aim for Jan 19 PoC kickoff.
[10:07] Priya: thanks, this was useful.
[10:10] Sarah: yes, thanks.
[10:12] Maya: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the items.
